On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA View image in fullscreen A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’ Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission. ‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast Read more Half of all peopl

My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
articles.raw_description: Upload at 2.4 Gbps, download at 600 Mbps, same cable and same adapter. Here's how I tracked it down to my Studio Display XDR, a tiny buffer, and a USB burst size of four packets. My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75% 2026-11-15 Oscar Molnar 8 min read (1684 words) # networking # debugging # apple # macOS # usb # unifi Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite! My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed. I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency. But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR . I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. articles.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
articles.raw_description: A quantization compiler that delivers 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size - ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant LookAtMyQuant LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage. On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site . The code is under the MIT license. LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai. The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time. The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release , packed for the Apple Silicon runtime. articles.raw_description: Often in life, your body is the one steering you. getting the mind to steer the body to steer you Nov 20, 2026 23 4 5 Share Often in life, your body is the one steering you. And sometimes, to get to do the thing you want, you can’t just convince yourself with reason or arguments, or will yourself, or do the exercises to get there - you need to learn the magic formula, the secret words, to trick the body into acting in a way that gets you the outcome you want. As a kid, spending time on the internet forums for bands I loved, I kept hearing about some magical book called The Easy Way to Stop Smoking by Allen Carr, that cured people of their smoking addiction. Middle-aged man after middle-aged man would praise the miracles of this book - not by the patch, not by gum, not by sheer will, only by reading this book could they quit smoking - and not only that, everyone they had given the book to had the same result. As a 12 year old, unable to find out what this book actually said, I spent hours thinking about this - trying to figure out what secret trick the book could be sharing that was so powerful. [to clarify, I have never smoked a cigarette in my life] So after countless nights thinking through this, this is what I came up with: you want to smoke because the craving feels bad, not because you actually want the cigarette. articles.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors
articles.raw_description: Free, self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors and AI investigation - sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer PcapAnalyzer Versión en español: README.es.md . Find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture (gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next. It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network. Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta. Try it without installing anything: https://pcap-analyzer-seven.vercel.app/#demo Download: https://sebaandrada6.gumroad.com/l/hspgx (free) or clone this repository. What it does 27 detectors that run on every capture, each with a severity and a next step: TCP: firewall blocks (SYN→RST), retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, loss and reordering, zero and full windows, resets after the handshake, slow handshakes. Path: PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, routing loops. Name and address services: unanswered or slow DNS, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN bursts, DHCP NAK / DECLINE / no answer, duplicate IPs, ARP storms. Applications: HTTP 4xx / 5xx and slow responses, TLS alerts, SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1. Tunnels: IPsec (IKE and ESP), WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo that are one-way, never answer a handshake or keep renegotiating. Security: port scans and sweeps, cleartext logins (FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, HTTP Basic; credentials are never stored or shown), Telnet / SMBv1 / SNMP v1-v2c, ARP spoofing, overlapping IP fragments.
